title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
authors: Xuanlyu Zhu, Feng Tian, Yang Zhong, Pengqi Zheng, Xiwen Bi, Ling Luo
abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

infographic.key_insight: The best system linked phenotype concepts to specific patients in full-text biomedical articles with an overall score of 0.7389, exceeding the baseline by 8.37 percentage points.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-specific phenotype extraction could support rare disease research and genotype–phenotype analysis, but this evaluation does not establish clinical benefit.
method: Recognize phenotype concepts in full-text biomedical articles.
Associate identified phenotypes with individual patients.
Top teams combined biomedical language models, LLMs, and ensemble strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark used 200 annotated PatientPheX articles covering 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient–phenotype associations.
infographic.watch_item: Patient attribution and phenotype normalization remain challenging, particularly in articles describing multiple patients.
infographic.paper_title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation
authors: Dai Lam Le, Minh Khoi Nguyen, Son Dinh Nguyen, Amir Reza Jafari, Viet Ha, Nguyen Son
abstract: Automated radiology report generation for multi-sequence brain MRI holds strong promise for alleviating radiologists' workload, yet it remains a demanding problem: brain MRI studies are inherently volumetric, each pulse sequence carries complementary diagnostic information, and annotated data are critically scarce for low-resource clinical languages. Existing brain MRI-report resources are still dominated by English reports, translated clinical text, or datasets adapted from task-specific imaging benchmarks, leaving routine low-resource clinical reporting and heterogeneous multi-sequence MRI protocols insufficiently represented. To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.

infographic.key_insight: ViBMR introduces a large-scale dataset pairing multi-sequence brain MRI with routine Vietnamese radiology reports to support report-generation research in a low-resource clinical language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset could support research toward reducing radiologists’ reporting workload, but the abstract does not establish clinical readiness.
method: Pair brain MRI studies with routine Vietnamese clinical reports.
Include T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences.
Evaluate representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: ViBMR contains 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series; the abstract describes comprehensive baseline evaluation but reports no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical accuracy and generalizability require further validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation

title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
authors: Ghulam Mudassir, Hameed Ullah Khan, Ahmad Sami Al-Shamayleh, Muhammad Faizan Khan, Muhammad Muqtasid, Moamin Abughazala
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

infographic.key_insight: This review maps bias in AI disease detection and highlights data diversity, explainability, and fairness-aware design as priorities for more equitable systems.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Recognizing bias in diagnostic AI may help clinicians and health systems evaluate whether tools perform equitably across patient populations.
method: Reviewed disease-detection AI studies within a stated 2015–2026 window.
Organized approaches by input data, model architecture, and bias type.
Examined identification and mitigation of algorithmic, demographic, model, and deployment bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 23 included articles from 64,389 records analyzed across seven digital libraries, without quantitative fairness or diagnostic-performance results.
infographic.watch_item: The review identifies research priorities but does not establish that any mitigation strategy reliably improves fairness in clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
authors: Jiayan Yang, Ad Feelders, Arno Siebes
abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-aware framework translates predicted patient deterioration risks into ICU staffing plans while balancing staffing costs against severe shortages.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support ICU workforce planning by accounting for uncertain demand, rigid shifts, and hiring delays.
method: Converts probabilistic risk predictions into uncertainty-aware staffing demand signals without changing the prediction model.
Uses Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to assess extreme shortage exposure.
Updates delay-constrained staffing decisions hourly through rolling-horizon scheduling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on realistic MIMIC-IV trajectories showed a favorable cost–shortage trade-off versus deterministic and reactive baselines, with stress testing under calibration drift.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports trajectory-based evaluation, not prospective deployment or demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing

title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning
authors: DM BAPPY, Eunsu Kim, Hanjoo Lee, Sung Hak Lee, Sangjeong Ahn
abstract: Learning across medical imaging modalities requires making use of images without paired text and accommodating new domains while retaining existing representations. We propose a medical vision-language technique built around an expandable bank of modality experts. Its Multiway Transformer combines shared visual computation with deterministically routed feed-forward experts and a separate text pathway. A modality-aware visual tokenizer supplies targets for masked pretraining on 19.4 million unpaired image rows across seven modalities; contrastive alignment then uses 3.23 million image-text pairs. Additional fundus and optical coherence tomography experts learn from paired data while the original image and text embedding paths remain frozen. With a ViT-Large backbone, the proposed technique achieves the best or tied-best result in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities: 10 of 11 zero-shot classification benchmarks, all 10 linear probes, and all four retrieval benchmarks. Mean balanced accuracy is 0.674 for zero-shot classification and 0.856 for linear probing, and mean bidirectional retrieval recall is 20.70%. A separate three-seed sequential experiment with matched adaptation data yields fundus and OCT retrieval gains of 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding fundus or pathology tasks. The preservation argument requires unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions, and feature-identity checks verify retention on evaluated inputs. The proposed technique provides a modular approach to learning and expanding medical vision-language representations.

infographic.key_insight: Expandable modality-specific experts enable medical vision-language learning across imaging domains while preserving existing representations when their computation paths remain unchanged.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support reusable image classification and retrieval tools across medical specialties, but clinical utility is not established by these benchmarks.
method: Combine shared visual computation, deterministically routed modality experts, and a separate text pathway.
Pretrain on unpaired images with modality-aware tokenization, then align image and text representations using paired data.
Add fundus and OCT experts while freezing the original image and text embedding paths.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training used 19.4 million unpaired image rows and 3.23 million image-text pairs; evaluation across nine modalities achieved best or tied-best results in 24 of 25 settings.
infographic.watch_item: Retention depends on unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions; feature-identity checks verify preservation only on evaluated inputs.
infographic.paper_title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning

title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains. In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation. Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM. We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance. This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.

infographic.key_insight: Three joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) formulations trained stably on longitudinal EHRs but consistently underperformed standard masked language modelling (MLM).
infographic.clinical_relevance: For research on patient representations from longitudinal EHRs, stable latent prediction alone did not yield performance competitive with MLM.
method: Adapted three JEPA formulations to predict EHR representations in latent space.
Compared their downstream performance with standard MLM using MIMIC-IV.
Examined how target size and heterogeneity affected prediction error.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-IV, all three JEPA formulations avoided representational collapse; larger targets increased prediction error, but reducing target size did not recover downstream performance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports evidence from MIMIC-IV only, leaving generalisability to other EHR datasets uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
authors: Soumya Ranjan Sahoo, Divya Bharti, Sanand Sasidharan
abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

infographic.key_insight: Longitudinal clinical retrieval should allocate limited evidence across time rather than repeatedly retrieve similar passages about the same diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help surface sparsely documented oncology transitions, such as recurrence or therapy changes, for clinical review.
method: Separate temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.
Compare Temporal-15 retrieval with a Global-50 baseline.
Test prompted precedence rules and fixed-budget temporal coverage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 13 queries over 20 patient records, Temporal-15 achieved milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for Global-50, but retrieved 496 versus 50 indexed units per query.
infographic.watch_item: Unequal retrieval budgets confound the recall gain, and without expert reference timelines, results measure retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report

title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT
authors: Emma Sarfati, Alexandre Bône, Pietro Gori, Sisi Yang, Marc-Michel Rohé, François Nicolas
abstract: Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS (p = 0.04)...

infographic.key_insight: In internal evaluation, dLI-RADS achieved 80% lesion-level accuracy versus 74% for LI-RADS, meeting the study’s non-inferiority criterion.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The method could support more consistent assessment of small liver lesions on multiphase CT, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Analyzes manually segmented liver lesions on multiphase CT.
Combines neural network predictions with handcrafted measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features.
Uses logistic regression to estimate hepatocellular carcinoma probability.
infographic.evidence_signal: This multicenter retrospective study excluded lesions larger than 40 mm and tested internal accuracy non-inferiority using 10,000 bootstrap repetitions with a 5% margin (p = 0.04).
infographic.watch_item: The supplied abstract does not report external sensitivity results, leaving generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner, Dongmin Bang, Tong Ding, Yuchang Su
abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

infographic.key_insight: Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter model, makes fast, probability-scored judgments from clinical records while a generalist language model formulates questions and synthesizes evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This division of labor could make population-scale record review and clinical-trial candidate screening more efficient.
method: Trained on 12.4 million question–answer pairs from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system.
Answers multiple typed questions in one forward pass without task-specific retraining, with probabilities to support routing uncertain cases to human review.
Pairs with a language-model agent for cited patient-history answers and trial-eligibility screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1 outperformed open decision models up to 27B parameters on 13 of 14 independently scored tasks; across 21 external datasets, aggregate performance approached the strongest tested 27B model with 6.4× faster inference in a matched workload.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective benchmark results do not establish clinical benefit; prospective validation and locally calibrated human-review thresholds are needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records

title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
authors: Mich-Seth Owusu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

infographic.key_insight: Africa-Papers introduces a 10.15-billion-token academic corpus designed to improve African representation in foundation-model training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its African medical scholarship could support more locally relevant medical NLP, but clinical benefits are not demonstrated in the abstract.
method: Combines DOAJ journals, CGIAR CGSpace, African-focused arXiv preprints, and OpenAlex-indexed publications.
Converts full texts into layout-aware Markdown preserving sections, equations, and tables.
Adds exact BPE token counts and a standardized eight-domain taxonomy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 844,807+ full-text papers across 879 Parquet shards, with DOAJ coverage spanning 31 African nations, but no downstream model evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Corpus scale alone does not establish medical accuracy or equitable coverage; downstream performance needs local validation.
infographic.paper_title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models

title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
authors: Tong Ding, Caiwei Tian, Dongmin Bang, Ming Y. Lu, Sophia J. Wagner, Andrew Zhang
abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

infographic.key_insight: MEDIATOR converts clinical text into shared discrete tokens, improving EHR prediction across hospitals without manual ontology mappings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Ontology-agnostic tokenization could help prediction models use more available EHR data when transferred between health systems.
method: Maps clinical concepts expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook.
Learns from synonyms, enriched descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs.
Supplies the resulting tokens to an EHR Transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 MIMIC-III tasks and 14 zero-shot eICU tasks, mean AUPRC improved by 4.0 and 8.6 points over the strongest prior tokenizer, respectively; MEDIATOR used all eICU events versus 13% for a closed-vocabulary tokenizer.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover two EHR datasets; broader generalizability and prospective clinical utility remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling

title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Joshua Placidi, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality--efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.

infographic.key_insight: Block diffusion offers a quality–efficiency trade-off for longitudinal EHR modelling, with one configuration delivering approximately 1.43× faster evaluation than autoregressive modelling.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More efficient EHR modelling could support clinical prediction research, but these findings do not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Compared block-based masked diffusion with autoregressive modelling on MIMIC-IV.
Matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions.
Varied block sizes and decoding strategies; assessed generative rollout and frozen linear probes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The B=8 configuration achieved approximately 1.43× faster evaluation, while frozen linear probes showed near-identical prediction performance across diffusion and autoregressive representations.
infographic.watch_item: Generative rollout generally underperformed autoregressive modelling, and larger denoising budgets produced diminishing returns.
infographic.paper_title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
authors: Frank-Peter Schilling, Daniel Barco, Philipp Denzel, Marc Stadelmann
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

infographic.key_insight: This review compares 3D diffusion models for medical imaging, highlighting their potential for high-fidelity, diverse image generation and their substantial resource demands.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Potential applications include CT, MRI, and PET data augmentation, reconstruction, inpainting, domain transfer, and artifact correction.
method: Comparative overview of existing 3D medical-image diffusion models.
Examines performance, limitations, and future research directions.
Discusses generation conditioned on patient characteristics, reports, masks, or other images.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review but provides no dataset sizes, quantitative evaluation results, or evidence of clinical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Volumetric modeling requires substantial memory, compute, and training data, which can constrain development and implementation.
infographic.paper_title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging

title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
authors: Rotem Gershon, Seffi Cohen, Dean Ariel, Havatzelet Bilavsky-Yarden, Amiel Sberro, Shai Yitzhaki
abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.

infographic.key_insight: Jev, a decision language model, showed competitive agreement with physician ratings and LLM judges while costing less and running faster than frontier judges.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Lower-cost, faster judging could make clinical AI output evaluation more scalable, but does not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Compared Jev’s structured judgments with frontier and open-weight LLM judges across four use cases.
Measured agreement with physician ratings on pediatric answers and HealthBench criteria.
Compared judgments with an LLM jury on MedHELM and a reference judge on HealthBench Professional.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 118 pediatric answers, Jev achieved Gwet’s AC2 of 0.50; it matched the HealthBench Professional reference judge on 91% of criteria, while frontier judges cost 73–294 times more and took 7–57 times longer.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement with an LLM jury or reference judge is not independent evidence of clinical correctness; broader physician validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI

title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
authors: Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras
abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

infographic.key_insight: Brain2Vec learns reusable 3D brain MRI representations that improve brain-age prediction and support downstream classification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could reduce labeled-data and computing requirements for structural brain MRI research, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Self-supervised pretraining on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans pooled from multiple studies.
Use pretrained weights for task-specific fine-tuning or frozen embeddings as standalone features.
Assess predictive performance, convergence speed, and anatomical interpretability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pretrained initialization improved brain-age accuracy and convergence versus random initialization; frozen embeddings outperformed anatomical volume features on four of five classification tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance or generalizability across deployment settings.
infographic.paper_title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI

title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

infographic.key_insight: CODA combines patient-cohort patterns with individual deviations to support multimodal clinical reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach aims to make EHR-based AI reasoning sensitive to both shared patient characteristics and patient-specific differences.
method: Uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts.
Represents each patient's deviation from a cohort prototype as a structured drift signal.
Integrates cohort and drift representations into a multimodal foundation model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability on real-world EHR benchmarks for closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety or prospective utility; cohort robustness across patient populations needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning

title: Plausible but Unimplantable: A Trustworthiness Audit of Shape Completion Foundation Models for Cranial Defect Reconstruction
authors: Marek Wodzinski, Kamil Kwarciak, Daria Hemmerling, Mateusz Daniol
abstract: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.

infographic.key_insight: None of the audited pretrained shape completion models produced implantable cranial reconstructions, even when outputs looked convincingly skull-like.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These models, used as released, did not meet the geometric requirements for cranial implant placement.
method: Audited three public pretrained models, including two foundation models, zero-shot.
Compared outputs with the patient's remaining bone as a do-nothing baseline.
Checked whether predictions added material without intersecting existing bone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 210 carved defects and 29 real cases, no audited model output was implantable; a task-specific volumetric comparator selected on these cases was implantable in all but one.
infographic.watch_item: At the evaluated point densities, implant thickness could not be determined from the point-cloud outputs, limiting their suitability for implant design.
infographic.paper_title: Plausible but Unimplantable: A Trustworthiness Audit of Shape Completion Foundation Models for Cranial Defect Reconstruction

title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
authors: Mohammed Saqlain
abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

infographic.key_insight: Biomedical claim-verification agents need relevant evidence, not merely valid citations: retrieval was the main bottleneck in this study.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Scientific assistants used in medicine should check whether cited papers support a claim, because a real PubMed ID does not establish relevance.
method: Evaluated SciFact claim verification with two language-model backbones and live PubMed search as the only tool.
Compared closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval, agent-written queries, and an oracle supplied with gold abstracts.
Audited citation existence and relevance using a cross-family LLM judge.
infographic.evidence_signal: Agent-written queries achieved 62% accuracy versus 49–59% for other realistic harnesses, without statistically significant differences; gold abstracts yielded 79–86%, while only 3 of 327 existing closed-book citations were judged relevant.
infographic.watch_item: The benchmark sample limited statistical power, and citation relevance was assessed by an LLM judge rather than established through clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
authors: Yiqing Shen, Mathias Unberath
abstract: Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered "more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.

infographic.key_insight: MedicalMLOmni uses evidence-guided AI agents to automate medical imaging model development, reporting the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A natural language interface could help medical researchers with limited coding expertise develop models, though benchmark performance does not establish clinical readiness.
method: Retrieve published results to guide model selection and configuration.
Run multiple agents in parallel to explore hyperparameter adjustments.
Automate training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports leading scores on 19 of 20 benchmarks and backbone-matched controls supporting framework-level gains; PMC-VQA favored a more broadly pretrained vision-language model.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance or reliability across real-world deployment settings.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis

title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
authors: Arvind Pillai, Alexis Roach, Jason Holden, Varsha D Badal, Subigya Nepal, Yu Yvonne Wu
abstract: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment measures how faithfully a therapist adheres to a treatment protocol, a critical determinant of positive patient outcomes. However, fidelity assessment is bottlenecked by manual expert review, rendering the process labor-intensive and unscalable. To scale therapy supervision and support clinician self-learning, we present an integrated application of large language models (LLMs) that automates psychotherapy fidelity workflows and generates actionable supervisory feedback from authentic, long-form clinical transcripts. We evaluate three open-weight models across multiple task decomposition configurations and reasoning strategies, demonstrating that evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation. Furthermore, we establish the framework's external construct validity on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT), where it reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills. Through a user study that evaluates the generated feedback, mental health experts indicate that the pipeline synthesizes actionable clinical feedback. Ultimately, our work offers a practical, scalable solution toward bridging the community mental health supervision gap.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-based workflow assesses psychotherapy fidelity and generates supervisory feedback, with evidence-first reasoning improving fidelity estimates.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could expand access to therapy supervision and support clinician learning, though improved patient outcomes were not established.
method: Analyze authentic, long-form therapy transcripts.
Compare three open-weight LLMs across task decompositions and reasoning strategies.
Generate fidelity assessments and actionable supervisory feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an independent RCT dataset, the framework distinguished CBT from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills; mental health experts also judged generated feedback actionable.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report sample sizes or quantitative performance, limiting assessment of reliability for routine supervision.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
